question: What did a survey of journals running free open-source publishing software find about how cheaply they operate?
title: A Survey of Scholarly Journals Using Open Journal Systems
answer: 998 journals using OJS: traditional peer review and acceptance rates, but mostly open access, fast-growing, many from developing countries, with extremely low operating budgets.

question: Is there a model where researchers pick a few papers at random, cite them and copy part of their reference lists?
title: A mathematical theory of citing
answer: The model of random-citing scientists, modified so the papers picked are recent; it reproduces the power-law distribution of citations to papers of the same year.

question: Roughly what share of articles indexed in 2011 could be read free from the journal publisher, immediately or after a delay?
title: Anatomy of open access publishing
answer: About 17% of the 1.66 million Scopus articles of 2011: 12% immediately and 5% within 12 months.

question: When biomedical authors pay their journal to make a paper free, how much extra citation does it get once other factors are controlled for?
title: Author-choice open-access publishing in the biological and medical literature
answer: A small but significant 17% across 11 journals; only 2 of the 11 showed a significant effect on their own, and the advantage was declining.

question: Within a single prestigious journal, were the papers made free on the journal site more likely to be cited than the rest?
title: Citation Advantage of Open Access Articles
answer: Yes: in PNAS, immediate OA articles were about twice as likely to be cited (odds ratio 2.1) 4 to 10 months after publication, rising to 2.9 at 10 to 16 months.

question: How much of the published particle physics literature is also posted as a preprint before or after publication?
title: Citing and reading behaviours in high-energy physics
answer: For over a decade, between 90% and 100% of articles in the main HEP journals have been available on arXiv.

question: Why might a nightclub let women in more cheaply than men?
title: Competition in two-sided markets
answer: Cross-group externalities: if men gain more from interacting with women than the reverse, platforms charge the side that brings more benefit to the other a lower price.

question: How well do reference managers like Mendeley and CiteULike cover the literature on bibliometrics?
title: Coverage and adoption of altmetrics sources in the bibliometric community
answer: Of 1,136 bibliometrics documents, 82% had at least one Mendeley bookmark, against 28% in CiteULike.

question: Do mentions of papers on social media go along with later citations, and which of those sources is common enough to matter?
title: Do Altmetrics Work? Twitter and Ten Other Social Web Services
answer: Six of the altmetrics associate with citations, but time effects can reverse the association, and only Twitter has enough coverage to be useful in practice.

question: Across philosophy, politics, engineering and maths, how much more often are papers that can be read free online cited?
title: Do Open-Access Articles Have a Greater Research Impact?
answer: From 45% more in philosophy to 51% in electrical engineering, 86% in political science and 91% in mathematics.

question: Does posting a mathematics paper as a preprint take readers away from the publisher's website?
title: Does the arXiv lead to higher citations and reduced publisher downloads for mathematics articles?
answer: Yes: arXiv-deposited articles received about 23% fewer publisher downloads, while getting 35% more citations.

question: Can how often a physics paper is downloaded early on tell us how often it will be cited later?
title: Earlier Web usage statistics as predictors of later citation impact
answer: Yes, moderately: over two years the correlation between downloads and citations was .42 for high energy physics, reaching its predictive power after about six months.

question: In astronomy, are conference papers posted as preprints cited as much as journal papers?
title: Demographic and Citation Trends in Astrophysical Journal papers and Preprints
answer: Posted proceedings are cited twice as often as unposted ones, but still about 20 times less than the average ApJ paper.

question: When a hundred psychology experiments were run again, how many gave the same significant result?
title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
answer: 36% of replications were significant, against 97% of the originals, and replication effects were about half the size of the original ones.

question: What happens to self-archiving rates when a university makes depositing papers compulsory?
title: Green and Gold Open Access Percentages and Growth, by Discipline
answer: A mandate roughly triples the percentage of green OA and speeds up its growth.

question: What proportion of scientists believe journals that publish free-to-read articles are good for their field?
title: Highlights from the SOAP project survey
answer: 89% of published researchers who answered; above 90% in most humanities and social sciences, around 80% in chemistry, astronomy, physics and engineering.

question: What mathematical form describes how many papers receive very large numbers of citations?
title: How popular is your paper? An empirical study of the citation distribution
answer: A power law in the tail, N(x) ~ x^-alpha with alpha close to 3, found from 783,339 ISI papers and 24,296 Physical Review D papers.

question: Is the higher citation rate of astrophysics papers on the preprint server really caused by their being free to read?
title: Open Access does not increase citations for research articles from The Astrophysical Journal
answer: No: the two-to-one advantage is due entirely to the nature and timing of the papers deposited, not to open access.

question: Do authors find putting their papers in a repository difficult or slow?
title: Open access self-archiving: An author study
answer: 20% found some difficulty with their first deposit, dropping to 9% later; 23% took over an hour the first time, 13% afterwards.

question: What two ingredients explain why some networks have a few hubs with a huge number of links?
title: Emergence of Scaling in Random Networks
answer: Growth, as networks expand by adding new vertices, and preferential attachment, as new vertices link to already well-connected ones.
